quote: The diagnosis was that C gave the programmer one tool for organising code
problem: The failures p2 just cited (OS/360, Multics) were not C programs. Ch5 said System/360 software was written in assembly, and OS/360 predates C (Fig 5.2: C in 1972), so the reader cannot see how those failures point to a flaw in C.
fix: say the evidence was the large C codebases of the late 1970s and 1980s, or that the diagnosis applies to any language whose only grouping tool is the function
reason: p2 cites OS/360 and Multics, neither a C program (OS/360 is 1965 assembly, Multics predates C), then p3 opens 'The diagnosis was that C...' with no bridge. The reader cannot see how those failures indict C.
judge_fix: Start p3: 'C programs of the 1980s reached the same size and hit the same wall. The diagnosis was that C gave the programmer one tool for organising code: the function.' Rest unchanged.

quote: If your subsystem had thirty types and three hundred functions
problem: From Ch5 the reader knows types only as char, int and double. Nobody has told them that each struct a programmer declares is a new type, so 'thirty types', and functions that 'belong to' types, do not make sense.
fix: say that each struct declares a new type of its own
reason: 'struct' appears for the first time in the preceding sentence, but 'types' is a new word for it; no earlier chapter teaches struct, so 'thirty types' arrives unprepared. Using the word just defined costs nothing.
judge_fix: 'If your subsystem had thirty structs and three hundred functions, the language had nothing to say about which functions belonged to which struct.'

quote: the classes and access rules of C++ were the answer
problem: The caption names 'classes and access rules' as the wall, but never explains them. The How it works strip, the only literal account of the wall, depends on 'private members' and 'the interface', and the reader knows neither, so they cannot say what the compiler actually refuses.
fix: in plain words: data marked private can be touched only by its class's own functions, and the compiler rejects any other code that tries
reason: Fig 6.1's strip uses 'private members' and 'the interface' before ch6-classes-p6 defines private, and 'interface' is never defined. The strip is the only literal account of the wall.
judge_fix: Strip bullet: '*The wall.* A class with private members (data that only the class's own functions may touch) lets the compiler refuse every touch from outside, cutting the lines that may exist.'

quote: Inheritance is one struct embedded inside another: a Circle object begins with a complete Shape
problem: The section never comes back to this. Fig 6.3 does not mark which part of the object (vptr, r = 2.0) is the Shape and which is the Circle. The 'Inheritance is layout' heading has no prose, and Fig 6.4 under it shows only vtable slots. So the reader cannot say what a 'complete Shape' inside a Circle holds, or why that lets a Shape pointer (p3, Fig 6.3's Shape* s) hold a Circle and still find the vptr.
fix: mark in Fig 6.3 the Shape part (the vptr first, then Shape's fields) and the Circle part (r), plus one clause: so a Shape pointer to any shape finds the vptr in the same place
reason: ch6-classes-p1 claims a Circle begins with a complete Shape, and the heading 'Inheritance is layout' promises it, but there is no prose under the heading and neither Fig 6.3 nor 6.4 shows which part is the Shape. The reason a Shape pointer finds the vptr in a Circle is never given.
judge_fix: Add a paragraph under 'Inheritance is layout': 'A Circle derives from Shape, so its object begins with a complete Shape (here just the vptr) followed by Circle's own field r. A Shape pointer to any shape therefore finds the vptr in the same place.' Optionally mark the Shape part and the Circle part in Fig 6.3.

quote: code written against an interface rather than an implementation
problem: 'Interface' and 'implementation' were only named in passing (ch6-complexity-p3 and its strip) and never explained, yet here they carry the definition of the bold taught term, polymorphism.
fix: plain words: print() is written for any Shape (anything with area() in slot 0), not for Circle's own formula
reason: The bold taught term is glossed with 'interface' and 'implementation', neither ever defined, though the sentence before it already gives the concrete meaning. Swapping in the concrete wording costs nothing.
judge_fix: Caption tail: 'that is **polymorphism**: code written for the general kind, Shape, not for any one shape's formula.'

quote: The constructor writes the vptr, so a Circle always points at Circle's table
problem: In Fig 6.3's How it works, 'constructor' appears as if the reader already knows it, but nothing so far defines it. So the reader cannot tell when or by what the vptr gets set, and the 'so' does not follow.
fix: 'the code that runs when new Circle(2.0) builds the object'
reason: 'Constructor' first appears in Fig 6.3's strip; it is defined only in ch6-raii-p3, a section later. The 'so' in the bullet depends on it.
judge_fix: '*Who sets it.* The constructor, the code that runs as `new Circle(2.0)` builds the object, writes the vptr, so a `Circle` always points at `Circle`'s table, whatever type of pointer holds it.'

quote: a determined caller can cast their way to it
problem: 'Cast' is never explained anywhere in the book so far, and the claim that a private field can be reached at runtime rests on it.
fix: 'treat the object's address as a plain pointer and read the bytes at the field's offset'
reason: 'Cast' appears nowhere else in Parts I and II, and the claim that a private field is reachable at runtime rests on it. The reader has pointers from Ch5, so plain words work.
judge_fix: '...a private field is just a field, and a determined caller can reach it through a plain pointer to the object's bytes.'

quote: Each resource is an object on the stack
problem: From ch3-stack-p4 and ch5-malloc-p2 the reader knows stack memory disappears with its frame on return and only heap memory needs freeing. So a buffer called 'an object on the stack' that still needs 'destructor: free buf' is a contradiction. The book never says that the small object on the stack holds a resource that lives somewhere else (buf's 1024 bytes on the heap, the open file, the mutex). p5's 'heap-allocated array' only hints at this, and only afterwards.
fix: 'Each resource is held by an object on the stack', plus a clause saying buf's 1024 bytes sit on the heap
reason: Caption says each resource 'is an object on the stack' but buf's 1024 bytes live on the heap; Ch3 and Ch5 taught that stack memory vanishes with the frame and only heap memory needs freeing. Accurate wording is one word.
judge_fix: Caption: 'Each resource is held by an object on the stack, acquired as its line runs and released by its destructor when the function exits, in reverse order.' Optionally add to p3 or the strip: 'buf's 1024 bytes sit on the heap; the vector object on the stack owns them.'

quote: a moved-from object is in a valid but unspecified state
problem: Fig 6.8 has just shown exactly what the moved-from v1 holds (empty, its pointers null), and this sentence says reading it is allowed. So the reader cannot see what is 'unspecified' or why this counts as a wound. The real harm, code that goes on using v1 as if it still held its data (a logic bug, not memory corruption), is never stated.
fix: say the standard promises only 'valid' (a vector happens to be left empty) and that the bug is code still relying on the old contents
reason: The strip says 'valid but unspecified' and 'reading it tells you nothing' right after Fig 6.8 shows v1 empty with null pointers. The reader cannot see what is unspecified or what goes wrong. The harm is code that goes on relying on the old contents.
judge_fix: 'Use-after-move: a moved-from object is left valid but in a state the standard does not fix (Fig 6.8's vector happens to be empty), so code that keeps using it as if it still held its data is wrong, and the compiler does not warn.'

quote: a use-after-free on a polymorphic object lets an attacker overwrite the vtable pointer
problem: In Chapter 5's use-after-free, the program writes through a stale pointer. Here the reader cannot see how an attacker gets to write the vptr. The skipped step: the freed object's chunk is handed to data the attacker supplies, so the attacker's bytes now sit where the vptr was, and the next virtual call through the stale pointer loads them.
fix: one clause: the freed chunk is refilled with attacker-supplied bytes, and the stale pointer's next virtual call reads them as the vptr
reason: Ch5's use-after-free shows a stale write corrupting the new owner. Here the direction reverses (the attacker's bytes become the vptr, read by the stale pointer's next virtual call), and the step is skipped. Also, only calls through that object are redirected, not 'every virtual call'.
judge_fix: 'Vtable corruption: when a polymorphic object is freed and its chunk is refilled with attacker-chosen bytes, the next virtual call through the stale pointer reads those bytes as the vtable pointer and jumps to attacker-chosen code, the modern descendant of the buffer overflow from Chapter 3.'

quote: enormous power (direct memory access, predictable cleanup, zero-cost abstraction)
problem: The reader learned 'direct memory access' in chBridge-io-p2/p4 as a defined term: a device reading and writing RAM by itself, without the CPU. Here the same phrase means a program reaching any address through pointers, so the reader stops and wonders how C gives the programmer DMA.
fix: reword as 'memory reached directly through pointers'
reason: 'Direct memory access' is a defined term in the Bridge (a device writing RAM without the CPU); p7 reuses the phrase for pointer access, which collides for a reader who just learned the term.
judge_fix: '(memory reached directly through pointers, predictable cleanup, zero-cost abstraction)'

quote: an iterator loop in C++98, a range-for in C++11, a single fold with no loop in C++23
problem: The fold with no loop is not new in C++23. C++98 already had std::accumulate (<numeric>, ISO 14882:1998 §26.4.1): `int total = std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0);` sums a vector in one call with no loop, and it is shorter than the C++23 fold_left line. The figure's C++98 panel and caption suggest C++98 forced a hand loop. The real C++23 gain is folding over the whole vector without naming two iterators.
fix: Caption: "Seven standards in twenty-five years, and the same task keeps getting simpler: an iterator loop in C++98, a range-for in C++11, a fold over the whole vector in C++23 (C++98's std::accumulate folded too, but between two iterators). The old forms still compile, so the language keeps growing while the recommended way to write it shrinks." The figure's C++23 gloss could also say "the whole of v, no iterators".
reason: std::accumulate has been in <numeric> since C++98 and sums a vector in one call, so 'a single fold with no loop in C++23' (caption) and the era framing of the figure imply C++98 forced a hand loop. The C++23 gain is folding over the whole vector without naming two iterators. Low severity but a C++ reader will notice. Not a kept-original figure.
judge_fix: Caption (ch6-modern-p6): "Seven standards in twenty-five years, and the same task keeps getting shorter: an iterator loop in C++98, a range-for in C++11, a fold over the whole vector, with no iterators to name, in C++23. The old forms still compile, so the language keeps growing while the recommended way to write it shrinks." Optional: the figure's C++23 gloss reads "the whole of v, no iterators".

quote: C offered no compiler-enforced way to wall parts off from one another
problem: C does have compiler-enforced walls, but they are coarse. A file-scope `static` function or variable has internal linkage, so no other source file can reach it. An opaque struct (declared in the header, defined only in its .c file) makes the compiler reject `p->field` in client code. That pattern is the textbook C abstract data type (Hanson, C Interfaces and Implementations, 1996). What C lacked was a wall around a type plus its functions inside one file, and access levels. p3's "nothing grouped functions" overstates in the same way.
fix: Second caption sentence: "C's only walls were the source file and the opaque struct, too coarse to tie a type to its functions, and the classes and access rules of C++ were the answer." Optionally, in p3: "Functions could group statements; only the source file grouped functions."
reason: The caption sentence 'C offered no compiler-enforced way to wall parts off' is literally false: file-scope static gives internal linkage and an opaque struct makes the compiler reject member access in client code (stdio's FILE). What C lacked was a wall around a type plus its functions, and access levels. p3's 'nothing grouped functions' overstates the same way, so repair both together (this also covers finding 11).
judge_fix: Fig 6.1 caption, second sentence: "C's only walls were the source file and the opaque struct, too coarse to tie a type to its functions, and the classes and access rules of C++ were the answer." And p3: "Functions could group statements; nothing but the source file grouped functions." (the following 'no language-level concept of module, no class, no interface' can stay).

quote: Simula 67 was designed in 1967 ... expressly for writing simulations
problem: That describes Simula I (1962–65). Dahl and Nygaard designed Simula 67 as a general-purpose language and moved simulation into a library class (SIMULATION). That generalisation is why its class and virtual mechanisms became the OO vocabulary. Source: Dahl and Nygaard, The Development of the SIMULA Languages (HOPL 1978), and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simula: "Simula 67 though was designed to be a general-purpose programming language".
fix: "Simula 67 was designed in 1967 by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard at the Norwegian Computing Center, growing a simulation language into a general-purpose one."
reason: Simula I (1962-65) was the simulation language. Simula 67 was designed as a general-purpose language, with simulation moved into a library class. Wikipedia (Simula): "Simula 67 though was designed to be a general-purpose programming language"; Dahl and Nygaard, The Development of the SIMULA Languages (HOPL 1978). The text conflicts with the source.
judge_fix: ch6-stroustrup-p2: "Simula 67 was designed in 1967 by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard at the Norwegian Computing Center, widening their simulation language into a general-purpose one." (rest of the paragraph unchanged).

quote: qsort vs std::sort, same algorithm, different cost
problem: The C standard does not say which algorithm qsort uses. glibc's qsort, the common Linux one, is a merge sort with a heapsort fallback: introsort was tried in 2023 and the stable mergesort was put back on 2024-01-15 (libc-alpha patch "stdlib: Reinstate stable mergesort implementation on qsort"). libstdc++'s std::sort is introsort. So 'same algorithm' is often false. The figure's real point, the path of one comparison, does not need it. The caption repeats it: "Same algorithm, a shorter path per comparison".
fix: Title: "qsort vs std::sort, same job, different cost"; caption: "Same sorting job, a shorter path per comparison, ..."
reason: The C standard fixes no algorithm for qsort. glibc's is a merge sort (introsort was tried in 2023 and the stable mergesort reinstated in January 2024), musl uses smoothsort, BSD/macOS a quicksort, while libstdc++'s std::sort is introsort. 'Same algorithm' is often false and appears in the figure title (label and svg title at part-2.html lines 3569 and 3571) and the caption. The figure's real point, the path of one comparison, does not need it.
judge_fix: Title: "Fig 6.6 · qsort vs std::sort, same job, different cost" (diagram-label and svg <title>). Caption ch6-zerocost-p3 last sentence: "Same sorting job, a shorter path per comparison, paid for with a separate copy of the sort for each comparison type."

quote: overflows for large values
problem: Large values alone do not overflow the subtraction (2,000,000,000 − 1,000,000,000 is fine). It overflows when the two operands are far apart, for example a large positive minus a large negative. That is how the ledger row for Fig 6.6 states it (§4g: "when the operands are far apart").
fix: "The usual comparator `return *(int*)a - *(int*)b;` overflows when the two values are far apart; `(x > y) - (x < y)` is safe."
reason: a - b does not overflow for two large values of the same sign; it overflows when the operands are far apart (e.g. INT_MAX - (-1)). 'Large values' misleads, and the §4g ledger row for Fig 6.6 already says 'far apart'. The text should match its own ledger.
judge_fix: Fig 6.6 strip 'A trap in C': "The usual comparator `return *(int*)a - *(int*)b;` overflows when the two values are far apart; `(x > y) - (x < y)` is safe."

quote: Scott Meyers wrote _Effective Modern C++_ (2014) because C++11 had overtaken much of his _Effective C++_
problem: Meyers chose not to revise Effective C++. He wrote a separate book with "42 all-new guidelines", which his site calls "a complement to Scott's existing books" (aristeia.com/books.html, GoingNative 2013 talk notes). Saying C++11 "overtook much of" Effective C++ invents a motive and suggests the older book was largely obsolete, which he did not say.
fix: "*The books.* Rather than revise _Effective C++_, Scott Meyers wrote a new one for C++11 and C++14, _Effective Modern C++_ (2014)."
reason: Meyers' own site (aristeia.com/books.html) presents Effective Modern C++ as 'a complement' to his existing books, with 42 new guidelines on C++11/14 features, not a response to Effective C++ being overtaken. The strip invents a motive and implies the older book was largely obsolete.
judge_fix: *The books.* Scott Meyers wrote _Effective Modern C++_ (2014) as a companion to _Effective C++_, for the features C++11 and C++14 added.

quote: By the late 1980s these languages ran most systems that mattered
problem: In the late 1980s C++ was barely out (Cfront 2.0 shipped in 1989). Much critical computing still ran on COBOL, Fortran, PL/I, assembly and Ada: banking, airlines, mainframe operating systems, defence. C was strong in UNIX, workstations and much PC software, but 'most systems that mattered' overclaims, especially for C++.
fix: "By the late 1980s these languages ran much of the world's systems software, and many programmers took this as the trade every language must make."
reason: 'Most systems that mattered' overclaims. Late 1980s critical computing still ran heavily on COBOL, Fortran, PL/I, assembly and Ada, and C++ was barely out (Cfront 2.0 in 1989; the book itself says C++ became dominant only by 2000). This also covers finding 25. C is defensible as the dominant language for new systems software, C++ is not.
judge_fix: ch6-modern-p7: "By the late 1980s C was the language of most new systems software, with C++ spreading behind it, and many programmers took this as the trade every language must make."

quote: lets the compiler refuse every touch that bypasses the interface
problem: The Fig 6.1 strip ('The wall') says the compiler refuses every bypass. ch6-classes-p6 says private is compile-time only and 'a determined caller can cast their way to it'. The two statements contradict each other.
fix: "*The wall.* A class with private members lets the compiler refuse every ordinary touch that bypasses the interface, cutting the lines that may exist."
reason: The Fig 6.1 strip says the compiler will 'refuse every touch that bypasses the interface', while ch6-classes-p6 states private is compile-time only and 'a determined caller can cast their way to it'. The book contradicts itself; 'every ordinary touch' keeps the figure's point (cutting the lines that may exist) and removes the conflict.
judge_fix: *The wall.* A class with private members lets the compiler refuse every ordinary touch that bypasses the interface, cutting the lines that may exist.

problem: Fig 6.4's title says 'same vptr slot, different function', but the slot is in the vtable. Each object's vptr is different, because it points at its own class's table. The drawing and the caption both say 'vtable slot 0', so the title contradicts them and uses 'vptr' for the wrong thing.
reason: The slot lives in the vtable; the vptr is the per-object pointer to it, and each class's vptr differs. The Fig 6.4 title says 'same vptr slot', contradicting the drawing, the caption ('slot 0 of each class's vtable') and the strip ('same slot of its vtable'). The term is misused in a title that teaches the terminology. Not a kept-original figure.
judge_fix: Rename in both the diagram-label and the svg <title> (part-2.html lines 3398 and 3400): "Fig 6.4 · Inheritance: same vtable slot, different function".

quote: Fig 6.4 · Inheritance: same vptr slot, different function
problem: The vptr is one pointer and has no slots. Slots belong to the vtable. The picture itself says 'vtable slot 0', and caption p5 says 'the same slot 0 of each class's vtable'. A reader who just learned the vptr/vtable distinction in Fig 6.3 is told the opposite in the title.
fix: Fig 6.4 · Inheritance: same vtable slot, different function (or the Polymorphism title from the previous finding).
reason: Fig 6.3 has just taught that the vptr is one pointer and the vtable is the array of slots. The Fig 6.4 label and svg <title> still say 'same vptr slot', while the picture itself says 'vtable slot 0'. The title contradicts the drawing.
judge_fix: Change the diagram-label and the svg <title> (svgt-part2-40) to: 'Fig 6.4 · Inheritance: same vtable slot, different function'.

quote: = 0 makes Shape::area pure virtual: Shape itself cannot be created, only its subclasses.
problem: The figure, its caption and the prose never show a declaration of Shape, so the reader has no '= 0' to look at. 'Pure virtual' is also taught nowhere. The item points at code that does not exist on the page.
fix: Replace the item with: '*The rule.* A `Shape` with no `area()` of its own cannot be created; only its subclasses can.' Or drop the item.
reason: The strip item points at '= 0' and 'Shape::area', but no Shape declaration appears in the prose, the picture or the caption. 'Pure virtual' is taught nowhere else in the book (grep confirms). The reader has no code to look at.
judge_fix: Replace the item with: '*The rule.* A `Shape` that leaves `area()` without a body of its own cannot itself be created; only its subclasses can.' Or drop the item.

quote: Calling s->area() loads the vptr, reads slot 0, and jumps there: two instructions, the second an indirect call.
problem: The caption repeats ch6-classes-p3 directly beside it. p3 already has the hidden per-object pointer to a per-class table and 'load the vtable pointer, index slot 0, jump to that address'. Pass 29's rule is that the prose keeps the explanation and the caption names the picture.
fix: Caption: 'Each Circle object carries a hidden vptr to Circle's one shared vtable; the two instructions at the bottom are the whole cost of `s->area()`.' Let p3 name the vptr: '...traditionally called the *vtable*; the hidden field is the *vptr*.'
reason: The second sentence of the Fig 6.3 caption ('loads the vptr, reads slot 0, and jumps there: two instructions...') restates the last sentence of ch6-classes-p3 and the two instructions drawn in the picture. The caption's one new job is naming the vptr, which the picture uses and p3 never names.
judge_fix: Caption: 'A class with virtual functions gives each object one hidden pointer, the vptr, to the vtable its whole class shares; `s->area()` costs the two instructions at the bottom, the second an indirect call.' Keep p3 as it is, apart from the finding 5 change.

quote: The call compiles to "load the vtable pointer, index slot 0, jump to that address."
problem: The prose gives three steps and the caption and picture say 'two instructions'. A careful reader counts and stops. In fact the slot-0 index is folded into `call [rax]`.
fix: The call compiles to two instructions: load the vtable pointer, then jump through slot 0.
reason: p3 gives three steps ('load the vtable pointer, index slot 0, jump') while the caption and picture say 'two instructions'. The slot index is folded into `call [rax]`, so a reader who counts finds a mismatch. Small, but a careful reader will stop on it.
judge_fix: p3 last sentence: 'The call compiles to two instructions: load the vtable pointer, then jump through slot 0.'

quote: a determined caller can cast their way to it
problem: 'Cast' has not been taught anywhere before this point (first use in the book). The sentence's point, that the wall is compile-time only, depends on it.
fix: a determined caller can still reach it through a pointer, as any C function could reach into a struct.
reason: 'Cast' as C/C++ jargon has not been taught anywhere before this point. The only other cast notation in the book is in Fig 6.6's strip, which is finding 22. The sentence's point (hiding is compile-time only) does not need it.
judge_fix: '...and a determined caller can still reach it through a pointer, as any C function could reach into a struct.'

quote: when the processor predicts the target, that is close to a direct call
problem: Branch prediction is first taught in Part V. Here the cost claim leans on it, and the reader cannot tell what 'predicts the target' means.
fix: *The cost.* One extra load and an indirect call; on a modern processor that is barely slower than a direct call.
reason: 'When the processor predicts the target' leans on branch prediction. In Parts I to IV, 'predict' appears only for Moore's law and the radar, and branch prediction is named first in Part V. The reader cannot say what is predicted. Explaining it would be expert detail beyond law 4, so the clause should go.
judge_fix: '*The cost.* One extra load and an indirect call; on a modern processor that is barely slower than a direct call.' (This is in the Fig 6.3 strip.)

quote: A virtual method, whose version is chosen while the program runs, costs one hidden pointer in each object
problem: This paragraph explains ahead of time what §03 explains in full: a class compiles to a struct plus functions (ch6-classes-p1/p2), and a virtual call costs a hidden pointer and a table call (ch6-classes-p3). The zero-cost promise is stated in stroustrup-p2, here, classes-p2 and zerocost-p1 as well. The same thing is explained twice across sections.
fix: Keep the first and last sentences only: 'What Stroustrup built was a deal: _you may add abstraction without losing speed_, because the compiler writes and checks the bookkeeping a C programmer would have written by hand.'
reason: The middle two sentences of ch6-stroustrup-p5 preview, in the same words, what ch6-classes-p2 and p3 then teach in full (struct plus functions, one hidden pointer and a table call). The zero-cost promise is also in stroustrup-p2 and zerocost-p1. The deal sentence works without the preview and is stronger without it.
judge_fix: 'What Stroustrup built was a deal: _you may add abstraction without losing speed_, because the compiler writes and checks the bookkeeping a C programmer would have written by hand.'

quote: Stroustrup's C with Classes (1979) became C++, standardised in 1998.
problem: The caption retells ch6-stroustrup-p3 (1979, the rename, the 1998 standard). The strip item 'Early compilers' repeats p3's 'a translator that turned the new constructs back into plain C' and 'Cfront, still worked by turning C++ into C'. The picture, the prose and the strip all say it.
fix: Caption: 'From Simula's classes to C++23, with the style turning from classic to modern at C++11.' Drop the 'Early compilers' item, or move its one new clause ('so C++ could run wherever a C compiler did') into p3.
reason: The Fig 6.2 caption retells stroustrup-p3 (1979, the rename, 1998) and the picture already draws those dates. The 'Early compilers' strip item repeats p3's 'translator that turned the new constructs back into plain C' and the Cfront sentence. The picture adds only the classic/modern style split at C++11.
judge_fix: Caption: 'From Simula's classes to C++23, with the style turning from classic to modern at C++11.' Drop the 'Early compilers' strip item. Optionally add to the end of p3's first sentence: ', so that C++ could run wherever a C compiler did'.

quote: Almost none of the old features were removed; the new ones were so much better
problem: Two things are said four times in the chapter. (1) The C++11 list (move semantics, lambdas, auto, smart pointers) appears in the Fig 6.2 caption, here, and the Fig 6.9 strip 'The two big ones'. (2) 'Old code still compiles, so the language only grows' appears in the Fig 6.2 caption ('keeping almost all older code compiling'), here, the Fig 6.9 caption ('The old forms still compile') and the Fig 6.9 strip ('Little is removed... the language only grows').
fix: Keep both in ch6-modern-p1. Fig 6.9 caption: 'One task in three eras: an iterator loop in C++98, a range-for in C++11, a single fold with no loop in C++23.' Fig 6.9 strip: cut the C++11 half of 'The two big ones' (keep C++20), and cut 'Little is removed' or reduce it to '`auto_ptr`, gone in C++17, is the rare removal.' Fig 6.2 caption as in the previous finding.
reason: The C++11 feature list appears in the Fig 6.2 caption, in modern-p1 and in the Fig 6.9 strip. 'Old code still compiles, so the language only grows' appears in the Fig 6.2 caption, in modern-p1, in the Fig 6.9 caption and in the Fig 6.9 strip. Keep p1 as the one telling. The Fig 6.9 strip should keep only what is new: C++20 and the auto_ptr removal.
judge_fix: Fig 6.9 caption: 'Seven standards in twenty-five years, and the same task keeps getting shorter: an iterator loop in C++98, a range-for in C++11, a single fold with no loop in C++23.' Strip 'The two big ones': 'C++11 and C++20 (concepts, modules, ranges, coroutines) each changed what "modern C++" means.' Strip 'Little is removed': '`auto_ptr`, gone in C++17, is a rare removal.' Fig 6.2 caption as in finding 10.

quote: each pair on a team needs a channel, so adding people to a late project makes it later
problem: The strip item 'The source' retells ch6-complexity-p2 (Brooks, 1975, adding people to a late project makes it later, because of communication). The caption's second sentence ('C offered no compiler-enforced way to wall parts off... classes and access rules of C++ were the answer') restates p3 and gives away p5.
fix: Caption: keep only the first sentence (Brooks's arithmetic and n(n − 1)/2). Strip: drop 'The source', which p2 already carries, and keep 'The same for code' and 'The wall'.
reason: The caption's second sentence restates ch6-complexity-p3 (no module or class in C) and gives away p5 (classes are the fix), and it sits right after p3. The strip item 'The source' retells p2 (Brooks 1975, adding people to a late project makes it later).
